On section 4-calling out by classes:
4. (1) The Governor in Council may from time to time by *proclamation call out on active service as aforesaid for the defence of Canada, either in Canada or beyond Canada, any class or subclass of men described in section three and all men within the class or subclass so called out shall, from the date of such proclamation, be deemed to be soldiers enlisted in the military forces of Canada and subject to military law for the duration of the present war, and of demobilization thereafter, save as hereinafter provided.
(2)	Meh so called out shall report and shall be placed on active service in the Canadian Expeditionary Force as may be set out in such proclamation or in regulations, but until so placed on active service, shall he deemed! to he on leave of absence without pay.
(3)	Any man by or in respect of whom an application for exemption is made as hereinafter provided, shall, so long as such application or any appeal in connection therewith is pending and during the currency of any exemption granted him, be deemed to be on leave of absence without pay.
(4)	Any man who is called out and who, without reasonable excuse, fails to report as aforesaid or to remain on active service where placed shall be guilty, according to the circumstances, of desertion, or of absenting himself without leave and shall he liable
(a) to he tried by court-martial and convicted and punished by imprisonment, for a term not exceeding three years, or
(h) on summary conviction to imprisonment for any term not exceeding three years.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER. I presume that the first subsection, means that all men called ont axe soldiers, unless exemption is granted?

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
Wihat is the
meaning of " leave of *absence without pay " in the subsection 2?

speechtext:
It may take some time to determine in just-what branch of active service a man 'should go. In the meantime it is not desirable that he should be kept from his ordinary vocation. He reports for duty, and until he is actually placed he is on leave of absence without pay. Again, in ease he applies for exemption, it may be that his case is not decided upon in time, and -until it is actually decided that he is a soldier and he is placed, he too is on leave of absence without pay. But he is a soldier all the same, and is liable to military discipline and liable to punishment if he deserts. * It is not wise to put him on the paylist in the meantime, for the reason that he is not actually on service.
Sir WILFRID*LAURIER:	That is, he
remains at home?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
When a man of 21 is
conscripted by law and appeals before a tribunal, and from that tribunal to the central appeal judge, I understand that by this section be is considered as a soldier without pay?

speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Has my hon. friend considered the length of time these processes of law should occupy before the' courts? Are special rules pf practice going to be framed to deal with these cases?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It was though t wise not to cover this by regulation for this reason. A member of the Supreme Court of Canada is to be made the central appeal judge, and he will have the final decision of all appeal cases. Consequently, it was thought vise that he himself should have the framing of regulations concerning appeals which will come ultimately to himself. The machinery is here in general, but no details are worked out as to time or otherwise, because the services of that Supreme Court judge will be utilized in w.orking them out.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
A case may he pending tor days and weeks and months. A rich man could keep the judicial machinery in motion as long as he liked, unless some limit were fixed. The central appeal judge of whom my hon. friend speaks may for good reasons be silent for a long time before adjudicating on a special case. That does not seem to me to be fair or just. It just comes back to what my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said very aptly
the other day, that the Bill seems to favour the rich against the poor. The madhineTy of law may be put in motion by the rich man, and an appeal may be pending for weeks and months, and although under the law he will be a conscript he will ibe considered as a soldier on leave of absence and wil be able to stay at home. It seems to me that if my hon. friend is not willing for the central appeal judge to frame those regulations, the Department ,of Justice should frame rules which would put a definite limit upon the time a case shall occupy from its inception to its close. Otherwise, the rich man who is unwilling to enlist could keep the wheels of justice rolling and rolling for. months and mpnths.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: If the regulations were poorly framed, that might be the case. I did not hear the address of the hon. member for Pictou, but I say now with all the emphasis, in my power that any one who can see in this Bill any attempt to favour the rich over the pooT is labouring under a very dangerous hallucination. How could any one get an advantage over the other under this Bill that he could not get under any Bill that human ingenuity might frame? The provisions for appeal are simple: We do not even go to the extent of stating the terms and conditions of appeal, but leave them to be framed by the central appeal judge, who is to be a member of the Supreme Court of Canada, none of whose members, I might point out, were appointed by this Government. Consequently, unless one imagines that that central appeal judge is going to frame such regulations as will allow the rich man by the use of money to prolong his appeal indefinitely, one can never imagine that this Bill is intended to favour the rich.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I did not make that suggestion. I understood my hon. friend to suggest that the Supreme Court judge might not take upon himself the framing of these regulations.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I do not anticipate that. I do not think there is a member of the Supreme Court who would not be glad in this crisis to- render any service in his power, and when it comes to framing rules of practice, that is clearly within his power; no one would be more capable of doing that. Let me say with all the finality in my power that it will undoubtedly be the design of those regulations so framed and to be approved by the Governor in Council, that no possible advantage shall be given the rich over the poor, and provision will



be made for expeditious and easy practice m appeal such as will put every man on an absolute level, as far as regulations can. The regulations, as I said, will be formulated by the central appeal judge, who is to-day a member of the Supreme Court. I can only repeat that any one who sees in this Bill anything designed to favour the rich over the poor is under a very dangerous hallucination.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Who will pay for the service of the subpoenas required by a person claiming exemption.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That will be a matter to be covered by regulations to be framed by the central appeal judge, who is a member of the Supreme Court of Canada. Inasmuch as very grave and heavy duties will be imposed on the central appeal judge, he is permitted, by a later clause, to name other judges at different points in Canada to perform the duties delegated to the central appeal judge. The great object, of course, is to ensure that it will be possible for the central appeal judge to efficiently execute the duties that are imposed upon him, but another object will be to enable him to see to it that such convenient methods of carrying out the appeals are made available as will enable the poor man to take an appeal as well as any one else. Regulations may be provided to meet all such conditions as to costs as they may at the time present themselves. It may be provided by the regulations, if deemed wise, that any one who is not in a position to pay his costs of service can have them paid for him. I do not say that will be done, but the Bill provides that if that is deemed wise by the central appeal judge it may be.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I have no doubt that the Government has no sinister design in this Bill. I am quite prepared to believe that my right hon. friend is filled with good intentions, but he knows there is a place which is said to be paved with good intentions, to which I might compare the Government with regard to this Bill but I shall not do so. I want to understand the meaning of this clause. The moment the proclamation issues calling out the men of a certain class, say between 20 and 25, they become soldiers, and they continue to be soldiers from that moment unless they are exempted from service. It will work out in this way: A man will have to report at a certain point, and then he will be obliged to present his reasons for exemption. If a father comes with his son and saysMy son is exempt because he is not of age, he

will be required to prove that before the tribunal. It may take some time; he may have the proof or he may not. In the province of Quebec it will not be very difficult, of course, because we have a very complete system of registration, but in other provinces it may not be so easy. Then there is an appeal from the decision, and from that appeal there is a second appeal. In the meantime, I presume, the father will be told: Take your boy home and keep him there until it is decided whether he is eligible or ineligible. I suppose it will work out in that way?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OP THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is it. I do not know that I can find any fault with my right hon. friend's understanding, except this: It is contemplated that the local tribunals will sit before the day for reporting; that is to say, the consideration of the application for exemption may'be completed bef ore the day for reporting, but if a case is not concluded on the day for reporting then the boy will be considered to be on leave of absence pending the decision upon his case.
